idiom_name: hand-written exchange over handles (pointer swap; struct copy through a temporary)
implementation_notes: C has no user-defined copy/move semantics, no destructors and no exceptions, so the guarantee the idiom exists to provide is vacuous: nothing throws, and the only non-local exit, longjmp, must not cross a frame whose ownership is half transferred. What remains is the exchange itself: for a handle-based type, swap the owning pointer (or a small struct of pointers) through a temporary so no allocation and no copy of the represented state happens, which is what keeps rollback paths in C-style error protocols cheap and failure-free. The classic C++ structure (member swap, ADL non-member, std::swap specialization, noexcept) has no C analogue - there are no namespaces to specialize into and no exception specification to write - so one swap function taking the handles by pointer replaces it, and the no-failure property lives in the header contract and in review.
pitfalls: memcpy-based struct exchange is undefined behaviour when the objects overlap (use memmove) and is wrong for structs that own pointers, where exchanging the pointer fields swaps ownership without respecting aliasing or reference counts.

C has no way to declare the guarantee: "this swap cannot fail" lives only in a comment or header contract, and a later change may add allocating work (strdup, malloc, logging) to the function without any compiler or caller noticing.

longjmp is C's only non-local exit; it must not jump out of a frame that has already exchanged one side of the state, and it skips the cleanup that a destructor would perform, so rollback helpers need explicit compensation code.
Swapping struct values by assignment copies the whole struct including inline arrays; for large types exchange a pointer to the state, not the state itself.
